GerdÅ¾iÅ«nas / LRT Western perceptions of Belarus remain clouded in uncertainty, despite its connections to the ongoing war in Ukraine. Understanding the hopes of Belarusian society will prove pivotal to properly engaging with the country when the conflict eventually comes to an end, Viktar Baranau writes for the New Eastern Europe magazine, partners of LRT English. Alaksandar Klacko recalls the first days of Russiaâs full-scale invasion without any romanticism. For him, the war began the moment he realised that missiles striking Ukrainian cities were being launched from the territory of his own country. Soon afterwards, he joined the Belarusian volunteers of the Kalinouski Regiment fighting on Ukraineâs side. He was later wounded and now lives in Lithuania. âWe understood that we were defending not only Ukraine. We were defending the future of Belarus as well,â he says. His story captures the contradiction that has shaped Belarus since February 2022. On one hand, Belarus became a crucial rear base for Russiaâs invasion: Russian troops attacked Kyiv from its territory, Belarusian infrastructure supports Russian logistics, military equipment is repaired there, and Russian soldiers receive treatment in Belarusian hospitals. On the other hand, thousands of Belarusians volunteered to help Ukrainian refugees, hundreds joined Ukrainian military units, and independent surveys consistently showed strong opposition to Belarus entering the war directly. Yet, this distinction has largely disappeared from Western analysis. Belarus is increasingly portrayed as little more than an extension of Russian foreign policy. This reflects an undeniable reality: the Lukashenko regime has become deeply integrated into Russiaâs war effort and, under international law, Belarus is complicit in the aggression against Ukraine. But this has also encouraged a broader assumption â that the interests of the regime, the Belarusian state and Belarusian society are essentially the same. That assumption obscures one of the most important political dynamics inside Belarus. While the regime has supported Russiaâs invasion, Belarusian society has largely rejected direct participation in the war. Understanding this gap is essential not only for interpreting Lukashenkoâs decisions but also for thinking about Belarusâs place in Europeâs future security architecture. Belarus being part of Russiaâs war is just one part of the story In recent weeks, the question of Belarusâs role in the war has once again come to the fore. After Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Russia was using navigation and communication systems located on Belarusian territory to strike Ukraine, he publicly demanded that Alexander Lukashenko stop their operation, threatening to destroy the facilities otherwise. Although Zelensky later reported that the equipment had been turned off, the situation itself once again returned Belarus to the headlines of international media and revived a familiar question: could Minsk become a direct participant in the war? A crowd waiting released Belarusian prisoners at the US Embassy in Vilnius last Saturday | AP Such questions have arisen regularly since February 2022. Every time Russia increases military activity or large-scale exercises are held on Belarusian territory, Western analysts again discuss the likelihood of a new offensive from the north of Ukraine. Belarus is perceived primarily as a potential Russian military springboard. This framing is quite understandable. If one judges solely by the actions of the Belarusian state, Belarus has indeed become one of the most important elements of the Russian military campaign. In January and February 2022, under the pretext of joint exercises, about 30,000 Russian servicemen were concentrated on Belarusian territory. It was from there that the advance on Kyiv began â the shortest invasion route on which the Russian command placed special bets. Russian troops used Belarusian airfields in Machulishchi, Baranovichi, and Lida, as well as radar stations and transport infrastructure. According to Ukrainian monitoring, in the first months of the war alone, at least 631 missiles were launched from Belarusian territory at Ukrainian cities. Cooperation was not limited to the first weeks of the invasion. Belarus transferred part of its equipment and ammunition from its stockpiles to Russia, provided enterprises for repairing damaged equipment, provided railway routes for supplying Russian troops, and gradually turned into an important element of the Russian military rear. According to Ukrainian intelligence, today more than five hundred Belarusian enterprises are in one way or another involved in producing goods for the Russian military-industrial complex â from electronics and optics to the repair of weapons and the production of components. Another symbol of this dependence was the deployment of Russian tactical nuclear weapons. For the first time since the collapse of the Soviet Union, Belarus has once again become a country on whose territory Russian nuclear warheads are located. Joint exercises using non-strategic nuclear weapons only cemented this role in Moscowâs strategy of nuclear blackmail. If one looks only at these facts, the conclusion seems obvious â Belarus is one of Russiaâs key allies in this war. âBelarus provides its territory, infrastructure, and resources to the Russian army. From the point of view of international law, this means complicity in aggression. There can be no two interpretations,â says the former Belarusian diplomat Pavel Slunkin. But it is precisely here, in his opinion, that Western analysis often takes a further step that is no longer so obvious. Given the Belarusian regimeâs participation in the war, the automatic conclusion is drawn that the interests of Moscow and Minsk completely coincide. âThis is the most common mistake,â says Slunkin. âYes, Russia and Belarus are in the same military space. Yes, the regimes support each other. But this does not mean that their interests fully coincide.â This conclusion has not only academic significance. Indeed, it directly affects how Europe assesses the risks of further escalation of the war. Minsk, Belarus | Pixabay If Belarus has completely lost its agency and all decisions in Minsk are made by the Kremlin, the obvious question arises: why, over three and a half years of war, has the Belarusian army never once crossed the Ukrainian border? This question is especially relevant today, when the likelihood of Belarusian territory being used again is actively discussed in the expert community. The answer is not that Lukashenko suddenly turned out to be a more independent politician than is commonly believed. According to Slunkin, the Belarusian leader acts primarily according to the logic of his own political survival. âFor Lukashenko, the current model is almost ideal. He provides Moscow with almost everything except the most expensive resource â his own army. He maintains loyalty to the Kremlin but at the same time avoids a decision that could destabilise the situation inside the country.â And the point here is not only Lukashenkoâs political calculation. Moscow itself, according to Slunkin, is not particularly interested in changing the current formula of Minskâs participation. When the question of sending Belarusian troops was being decided in 2022, the Kremlin was convinced that the operation would end quickly and on its own â there was no need to share the future victory with an ally. Since then, the calculation has changed, but the conclusion has remained the same: Russia does not need 15,000 to 20,000 unmotivated Belarusian soldiers against a Ukrainian army that has accumulated combat experience over three years of war unparalleled in Europe. A secure rear is far more valuable to Moscow: oil refineries that are not bombed, airfields and hospitals that operate without the threat of strikes, warehouses and logistics that simply function without failures. In addition, Belarusâs position remains an additional lever of pressure on the Baltic states and Poland. To exchange this quiet haven for a handful of additional bayonets that would turn Belarus itself into a legitimate military target for Ukraine would, from the Kremlinâs point of view, be simply pointless. It is here that the difference between the regime and society becomes noticeable. Lukashenko did not refuse to participate in the war. He refused only the form of participation that could threaten the stability of his own power. And in order to understand why this risk turned out to be so serious, it is necessary to look beyond the regime itself and at Belarusian society â the part of Belarus that has practically disappeared from western discussion about the war. The regime entered the war. Society did not One circumstance that western deliberations about Belarus have almost completely left out is public opinion. In authoritarian states, public opinion is often disregarded. When one person makes all the key decisions, it seems logical to focus exclusively on his motives. However, in the case of Belarus, it is precisely societal attitudes that largely explain why the countryâs participation in the war turned out to be significantly more limited than many expected in the spring of 2022. Independent sociological research consistently records the same trend: the majority of Belarusians do not support their countryâs direct involvement in the war in Ukraine. According to the latest Chatham House and Center of New Ideas surveys, only 14 percent of respondents express direct support for the Russian invasion, while overall about a third (27 percent) approve or rather approve of Russiaâs military actions. Even more telling is the attitude toward the possible sending of the Belarusian army to Ukraine: only 9 percent of Belarusians believe that their army should take part in the war. Belarussians in Lithuania | B. GerdÅ¾iÅ«nas / LRT At first glance, this looks paradoxical. Belarusian society remains one of the most pro-Russian in Europe. As of November 2025, 44 per cent of Belarusians support a geopolitical union with Russia. For a significant part of the population, it remains the main political and cultural partner. However, this sympathy almost does not convert into support for the war. The Belarusian sociologist Daria Urban explains that it is here that many external observers make a fundamental mistake: âIn the West, there is often a simplified logic: if Belarusians have a positive attitude toward Russia and choose an alliance with it, then they must automatically support the Russian war as well. But this is not the case. âThe high figure of supporters of a union with the Russian Federation is largely the result of people simply being left with no other choice. Under conditions of total isolation, Russia is perceived as the path of least resistance, as the only tangible reality, and not at all as a conscious ideological choice in favour of war.â According to Urban, Belarusiansâ attitude toward Russia and their attitude toward the war exist in completely different planes: âSociety is not sociologically monolithic; different groups of people live in non-overlapping information and value planes. And the fact that a person does not want their country to go to war does not mean automatic legitimisation of Lukashenko. Belarusians are mentally not ready to enter this conflict. We have the popular expression ânever againâ embedded at the subconscious level, so people en masse will not go to fight.â In her assessment, the truth lies somewhere in the middle. The average person adapts to the system not out of love for it, but because of the lack of an alternative: Lukashenko himself also does not want the direct participation of his army, but allows the regime to participate in the war only to the extent that it does not require the mobilisation of society. He presents this line as his own main achievement â supposedly he âpreserved peaceâ. âMost people perceive Russia as a close state, but at the same time categorically do not want Belarus to become a direct participant in hostilities. For people, these are completely different, unrelated questions.â After the mass protests of 2020, Lukashenkoâs regime found itself in a deep crisis of legitimacy. Russiaâs full-scale invasion did not automatically restore it. Rather, a new unspoken social compromise emerged: many were ready to tolerate continued authoritarian rule only as long as Belarus was not directly drawn into the war. This is precisely why Lukashenko found himself in a dual position: Moscow expects maximum support, but the decision to send the army would mean a head-on collision with the sentiments of his own society. This does not mean that public opinion determines the policy of an authoritarian regime. But it determines the price of political decisions. This is precisely why, explains Slunkin, the refusal of direct army participation should not be perceived as an example of Minskâs independent foreign policy. âThis was a decision not in the interests of Ukraine and not even in the interests of Europe. It was a decision in the interests of preserving power.â As a result, a situation has arisen that fits poorly into the scheme familiar to Western analysis. The Belarusian regime has become a full participant in the Russian war machine. Belarusian society has not. Russia's war against Ukraine | AP It is this contradiction that explains much of what has happened in the country over the past three years: from the mass unwillingness to fight to the growth in popularity of the narrative that Lukashenko supposedly âpreserved peaceâ for Belarus. But if society differs so much from the regime, why does the West continue to see Belarus as only one monolithic object? Daria Urban explains the roots of this blindness through how the West in general constructs information about the region: âWe recently conducted a study of the media image of Belarus and discovered a terrible thing: Belarus has no clear image in the West. Its society is perceived as some kind of monolithic organism, a single whole. There is no articulated position; Belarus is written about infrequently. https://www.theconstructionindex.co.uk/t.text: The Digger Blog Polish team crowned world leaders in Volvo support Share Share Share Share Polish team crowned world leaders in Volvo support Equipment technicians from Volvo Maszyny Budowlane Poland have been acclaimed as the world's best aftersales team at a Volvo CE competition in Sweden. The Volvo CE Masters has, for 35 years, judged authorised dealer teams on the skills needed to cut downtime on site. They are assessed for the speed and accuracy of their machine diagnostics, deep product knowledge across Volvo CE's equipment range, and the ability to work efficiently and effectively as a team under pressure. This year, almost 3,000 individuals participated in the competition, the largest pool of entrants in the event's history. Volvo Maszyny Budowlane's team, dubbed the Golden Boys , comprised Michał Pietrzak, Piotr Lebda, Michał Motycki, Remigiusz Piątek and Paweł Olkowski. They arrived at the Eskilstuna competition ground after winning the European Regional Finals. Kamila Czaja, head of retail operations, Volvo Maszyny Budowlane, said, "This is an incredibly proud moment for all of us. Becoming Volvo Masters World Champions is a remarkable achievement, but what makes it truly special is the team behind it. Their expertise, passion, commitment and trust in one another made this success possible. I am extremely proud of what they have achieved together and sincerely grateful to everyone who contributed along the way." INTERNATIONAL World Watch By: Agencies Date: October 12, 2026 Share post: WhatsApp Facebook X ReddIt Telegram Linkedin North Korea celebrates 81st anniversary of Workers’ Party Seoul, Oct 11: North Korea has held a celebratory performance for the 81st founding anniversary of the Workers’ Party of Korea, with leader Kim Jong-un in attendance, state media reported on Sunday. Patriotic songs, acrobatics and dance filled Pyongyang Indoor Stadium the previous day in a show that stressed loyalty to the party and Kim, reports Yonhap, quoting Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). Kim, whom the article described as “representing the dignity and mightiness” of the country, waved to the audience “as a token of his congratulations to all the participants on the party founding day” and expressed satisfaction with the performance, the KCNA said. A photo released by the KCNA shows Kim’s wife, Ri Sol-ju, and daughter, Kim Ju-ae, accompanying him. Diplomatic envoys and members of foreign missions sat alongside senior party and military officials and Pyongyang citizens, according to the report. Kim did not issue a statement marking the anniversary. The performance capped a series of events and gatherings marking this year’s anniversary, which were modest in scale. (IANS) Poland school attacks fueled by glorification of violence Warsaw, Oct 11 : The attacks at Polish schools over the past week were “spontaneous acts” driven by the online “glorification of violence,” Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sunday. Three attacks at schools in the Mazovian province in central Poland took place within four days this week, leaving one dead and many wounded, including children. By Sunday morning, police had detained 117 people across Poland for carrying knives or other dangerous weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students. Some 64,000 schools were checked. “We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale,” Tusk said on Sunday morning, during a crisis meeting with government and security services. “These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity.” “In the past years and months, we have noted – globally and in Poland – a rise in the fascination with violence.” (AP) Nine killed in Pennsylvania shooting New York, Oct 11: Nine people, including two children, were dead following a shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania, US media reported. Police were called to Perry Street on Friday evening after eyewitnesses reported seeing a man firing a gun before he entered a home, according to media reports on Saturday (local time). Two women were found dead in the street, and more victims were later found dead inside the home, reports Xinhua, quoting Erie News Now. Police said that the suspect was also found dead with an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. The City of Erie authorities said Saturday that all nine deaths occurred before police arrived at the scene. No additional gunshots were fired after police arrived. Police have not yet released the identities of those killed or discussed a possible motive. Earlier this month, an 18-year-old Minnesota man was charged with a firearm offence.
